page: Microsoft Azure D4als_v6 is a compute-oriented virtual machine belonging to the Dalv6 server family, powered by the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture with an AMD EPYC 9V74 processor operating at a base frequency of 3.7 GHz. The configuration provides 4 dedicated vCPUs mapped from 2 physical cores with multithreading enabled. The CPU cache architecture includes 32 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 32 MB of L3 cache. It supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 (including AVX512F, AVX512_VNNI, and AVX512_BF16) and cryptographic acceleration via AES, VAES, and SHA_NI. The instance is provisioned with 8.0 GB of system memory, yielding a low memory-to-vCPU ratio of 2.0 GB per core. There is no bundled local storage or GPU hardware, though the instance is premium storage capable.

In benchmark evaluations, the AMD EPYC processor demonstrates strong single-core performance, ranking in the top 25% for both stress-ng single-core and Geekbench single-core tests, as well as Geekbench text processing. Multi-core performance is average, placing in the middle 50% for stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and PassMark CPU tests. However, the low-memory configuration introduces significant performance tradeoffs. Memory bandwidth is weak, with read-only operations scoring in the bottom 25% and PassMark memory performance falling into the bottom 10%. This memory bottleneck impacts memory-intensive workloads, as evidenced by weak performance in software compilation, ray tracing, and database operations. LLM inference speeds are average for small models but drop to poor or weak for medium 7B models.

The D4als_v6 offers a cost-efficient profile for workloads that require dedicated, high-clock-speed CPU execution without demanding large memory footprints or local storage. Because it lacks bundled local SSDs and features a low memory-to-vCPU ratio, it minimizes overhead costs associated with unused resources. This makes it appropriate for CPU-bound tasks with small working sets, such as static web serving, single-threaded text processing, lightweight Redis caching, and basic microservices. It is less appropriate for memory-intensive databases, large-scale software compilation, or complex data science tasks.
